lesson.title: The sensors in your phone
lesson.subtitle: Motion, light, location, and a camera made of numbers

video.title: The sensors in your phone
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Joseph — computer studies teacher (main character)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph turns a phone sideways and the video on it turns too; then he lifts it to his ear and the screen goes black.
scenes.animation: The phone rotates; the screen fades to black at his ear.
scenes.narration: Turn your phone sideways, and the video turns too. Hold it to your ear in a call, and the screen goes dark. Who's telling it? Its sensors. Let's find them.

scenes.visual: Darsi title card with the IoT track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: the sensors in your phone, and how your camera turns light into numbers.

scenes.visual: A see-through phone with a tiny chip glowing inside; an arrow points down; the phone shakes, then walks with footprints behind it.
scenes.animation: The arrow stays pointing down as the phone tilts; footprints count up.
scenes.narration: First, the motion sensor, or accelerometer. It feels which way is down, and every shake and step. That's how your screen turns and steps get counted.

scenes.visual: Close-up of the top of a phone: two tiny dots beside the front camera. A sun moves across and the screen brightens; a hand comes close.
scenes.animation: The screen brightens with the sun; a ring pulses as the hand nears.
scenes.on_screen_text: Two tiny sensors at the top
scenes.narration: Near the top of the screen sit two tiny sensors. The light sensor measures how bright it is, and sets the screen to match. The proximity sensor, the nearness sensor, notices when something is very close.

scenes.visual: A map turning to face north; satellites high above sending signals down to a phone; a finger tapping a screen.
scenes.animation: Each picture pops in as it is named.
scenes.narration: There's more. A compass sensor feels the Earth's magnetism, so maps point the right way. The GPS listens to satellites to find where you are. Microphones hear you, and the touch screen feels your finger.

scenes.visual: Amina holding a phone to her ear; the screen is dark. Three answer cards drop in.
scenes.animation: Cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! You're on a call, and the screen goes dark at your ear. Which sensor noticed your ear?

scenes.visual: Faint red waves leave the top of the phone, hit an ear and bounce back; the screen goes dark.
scenes.animation: Waves go out, bounce back; the screen fades out.
scenes.narration: The proximity sensor. On most phones, it sends out invisible infrared light and notices it bounce back off your ear. Then the screen switches off, so your cheek can't tap buttons.

scenes.visual: A phone camera lens opens up into a huge grid of tiny squares, each catching a little light.
scenes.animation: Zoom into the lens; the grid fills the screen.
scenes.narration: Now the biggest sensor in your phone: the camera. It's millions of tiny light sensors in a grid, each measuring the light that lands on it. A twelve-megapixel camera has about twelve million.

scenes.visual: One square of a photo zooms out of the picture and shows three numbers: red, green and blue.
scenes.animation: The square lifts out; its three numbers count in.
scenes.on_screen_text: A photo is a grid of numbers
scenes.narration: Each tiny square of a photo is a pixel. Your phone stores each pixel as numbers for its red, green and blue light. So to your phone, a photo is a grid of numbers. Change them, and the picture changes.

scenes.visual: A tiled wall mosaic: close up, coloured squares; the camera pulls back and a smiling face appears.
scenes.animation: Slow pull-back from the tiles to the whole face.
scenes.narration: It's like a mosaic of small tiles. Close up, you see only squares. Step back, and you see a face. Zoom into a photo, and you'll find the squares too.

scenes.visual: A phone screen with a live graph; students hold it up at break, by a window, and lay it flat on a desk.
scenes.animation: The graph line moves with each place.
scenes.on_screen_text: Your phone as a science lab
scenes.narration: You can read your phone's sensors yourself. A free app called phyphox shows them as numbers and graphs. Measure how loud break is, how bright the window is, or whether your desk is level.

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor holds up a phone that has just taken a photo of the school garden. Two answer cards bounce in.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. You take a photo with a twelve-megapixel camera. What does your phone actually store?

scenes.visual: The phone's sensors light up one by one on a see-through phone.
scenes.narration: About twelve million pixels, each stored as numbers. Remember: motion, proximity and light sensors, a compass and GPS. And a camera: millions of light sensors making a grid of numbers.

scenes.visual: A student measures by a window and at the back of the room; another shades squares on squared paper and writes numbers in them.
scenes.animation: Numbers appear in the squares one row at a time.
scenes.narration: Try it tomorrow: with a parent's OK, open phyphox or a compass app, and measure one thing in two places. Write both numbers with their units. No phone? Draw a picture on squared paper, with a number in each square. Next time: measuring it right.

checkpoints.prompt: In a call, the screen goes dark at your ear. Which sensor noticed your ear?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — the proximity sensor notices something very close, like your ear, and the phone switches the screen off.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — it does get darker by your ear, but the light sensor only sets the brightness. The proximity sensor notices something very close and switches the screen off.

checkpoints.prompt: You take a photo with a 12-megapixel camera. What does the phone actually store?

options.text: About 12 million pixels, each stored as numbers
A tiny copy of the scene, like a printed photo

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — each pixel is stored as numbers for its red, green and blue light: millions of numbers in a grid.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — there's no tiny picture inside. The light sensors give numbers, and the phone stores every pixel as numbers.
